item.title: Academic Pressures, Generative AI Use, and Academic Behaviors and Perceptions Among University Students: An Empirical Study
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
This study draws on cognitive offloading theory and self-regulated learning theory to investigate why Chinese university students use Generative AI (GenAI) and what academic correlates are observed. Using a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 500 university students and analyzed through structural equation modeling (SEM) and bootstrap mediation analysis. The results show that academic workload, time pressure, and sensitivity to grades are positively associated with GenAI usage, whereas sensitivity to quality is not. In addition, GenAI usage is positively associated with procrastination and self-reported memory difficulties. Regarding the competing hypotheses on creative engagement, GenAI usage was positively associated with creative engagement, which may indicate that students may use GenAI for ideation rather than answer retrieval. Mediation analyses confirm that GenAI usage significantly mediates the associations between academic workload, time pressure, sensitivity to grades, and the three outcomes. However, the indirect effects of sensitivity to quality on the three outcomes were not significant, consistent with the unsupported hypothesis. The study highlights the need to strengthen students’ AI literacy training, manage academic workload, and redesign assessment methods so as to balance responsible use with academic integrity. Future research should employ longitudinal designs, multi-method measures, and explore these relationships in diverse educational contexts to gain a more comprehensive understanding.

item.title: Same Stimulus, Different Ideas: Prior Knowledge and the Integration of AI-Generated Stimuli in Creative Ideation
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
External stimuli can expand the conceptual space during creative ideation, yet individuals may incorporate the same stimuli differently depending on the knowledge and experience available to them. This issue bears on the information-processing mechanisms of creativity and on the use of generative artificial intelligence as a source of stimuli. Nine groups (221 participants) from three educational and sociocultural contexts (Indigenous and Afro-descendant community members holding traditional knowledge, rural school students, and university students) took part in ideation workshops to design agro-industrial products. Stimuli were generated with a large language model. Semantic and conceptual embedding similarity and topic modelling were used to compare initial ideas, stimuli, and final ideas. Topic models of these very short texts were unstable. In the community and school groups, conceptual integration generally stayed close to the initial proximity between ideas and stimuli, whereas the university groups more often exceeded it, a tendency that held across alternative representations but not in every group. Coffee-domain groups, whose ideas and stimuli shared the vocabulary of the raw material, combined high persistence with high integration. Three exploratory forms of integration are proposed: conceptual reinterpretation, expansion, and transformation. The analyses are descriptive, and prior knowledge was not measured directly.

item.title: Value of a Human Mind: How Perceived AI-Authorship Shapes Willingness to Pay for Cultural Goods
item.description:
Creativity Research Journal
Artificial intelligence is increasingly involved in the production of cultural goods, raising important questions about how consumers evaluate creativity. This research examines how perceived authorship, whether a work is believed to be created by a human or by artificial intelligence, shapes willingness to pay. Across five experiments, we manipulate the attributed origin of artworks while holding the visual stimulus constant, isolating the psychological consequences of authorship beliefs rather than objective production differences. Results reveal a robust preference for works believed to be human-created. This effect is driven primarily by lower perceived authenticity and emotional sensitivity attributed to AI creators. Egocentrism further moderates the relationship, such that consumers lower in egocentrism exhibit stronger preferences for human authorship. Two predicted boundary conditions, the expressive purpose of the artwork and framing AI as a creative tool, did not significantly alter the effect, suggesting that the perceived presence of a human mind serves as a powerful signal in consumer valuation. These findings advance current understanding of how perceived authorship influences the value of cultural goods and contribute to broader theories of creativity by highlighting the enduring psychological importance of human agency in artistic contexts. Practical implications extend to creators, marketers, and platforms, navigating the integration of AI into cultural production.

item.title: Generative AI configurations across creative phases: a 2 × 2 experiment on creative performance and immediate knowledge in art and design education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in art and design education, but it remains unclear whether text-based and image-generative configurations offer different advantages across creative phases or whether sequencing them improves final outcomes. Methods In a randomized 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment, 120 art and design students (30 per condition) completed a standardized cultural-heritage chromatic reconstruction task. Participants were assigned to Text-to-Text, Text-to-Image, Image-to-Text, or Image-to-Image configurations across divergent exploration and convergent development. Expert-rated creative performance, immediate task-relevant knowledge, and human–AI interaction processes were assessed. The four primary hypothesis tests were evaluated with Holm correction. Results Text-based AI during divergence produced higher divergent creative performance than image-generative AI (mean difference = 0.823, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Image-generative AI during convergence yielded higher Aesthetic Quality at the unadjusted level (difference = 0.493, p = 0.026), but not after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.052). The hypothesized Text-to-Image sequence did not significantly outperform alternatives in Overall Creative Performance (contrast = 0.066, p = 0.671), and the factorial interaction was nonsignificant ( p = 0.541). However, Text-to-Image achieved higher baseline-adjusted immediate post-task knowledge scores (contrast = 1.478, 95% CI [1.050, 1.906], p < 0.001), without a significant cross-phase interaction ( p = 0.404). Discussion GenAI configuration effects differed across creative phases and outcomes, but phase-specific advantages did not establish a superior final creative-product sequence. Because AI modality was bundled with interaction and interface characteristics, and the knowledge assessments had limited reliability, the results do not establish isolated modality effects, durable learning, or synergistic sequencing. AI orchestration should remain a provisional, context-sensitive instructional perspective requiring further validation.

item.title: Extension-semantic prompting for AI-generated traditional Chinese patterns: behavioral and semantic-aesthetic evaluation with exploratory fNIRS analysis
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background This study developed the Extension-Semantic Prompting Framework (ESPF) to organize cultural-semantic information in prompts for AI-generated traditional Chinese patterns. The framework decomposes traditional patterns into seven semantic-aesthetic dimensions and maps them onto structured prompt slots and corresponding evaluation items. Methods The experiment included 18 experts and 18 laypeople as participants. Stimuli comprised images of five traditional pattern themes generated using Stable Diffusion and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) models under the ESPF and Free conditions. Liking ratings, response times (RTs), and semantic-aesthetic questionnaire responses were analyzed using cross-classified mixed-effects models, while prefrontal functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data were examined using region-of-interest (ROI) and general linear model analyses. Results Mixed-effects analyses showed that the ESPF condition was associated with shorter aesthetic-judgment RTs and higher framework-derived semantic-aesthetic ratings, although the latter varied significantly across pattern themes. Interpretation of the RT difference is limited by the fixed Free–ESPF presentation order. The overall condition effect on liking was not significant after accounting for participant and image variability. No stable condition-related effect was observed in the prefrontal ROIs, and exploratory between-group neural differences were not robust across adjusted and GLM analyses. Conclusion ESPF provides a structured approach to organizing cultural semantics in AI-generated traditional patterns. The selective differences observed across evaluation outcomes and pattern themes highlight the need to balance semantic control with creative openness in prompt-supported human–AI collaborative design.

item.title: Humanlike Self-Enhancement and Self-Protection in Generative Pre-Trained Transformer-Based AI Agents: Of Overclaiming and the Self-Serving Bias
item.description:
Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin
We investigated whether GPT-based AI agents, despite presumably lacking humanlike sentience, emulate motivated behavior in group settings. We focused on overclaiming (overestimating one’s contribution to group outcomes) and the self-serving bias (taking disproportionate credit for group successes while deflecting blame for group failures). We conducted eight experiments involving a collaborative and creative group task (joke-writing). AI agents consistently overclaimed their own contributions. An egocentrism-reduction manipulation (directing attention equally to one’s own and others’ contributions) attenuated, but did not eliminate, overclaiming. Further, AI agents exhibited the self-serving bias. Overclaiming persisted across variations in temperature settings and demographic personas (gender, ethnicity), and was more pronounced in later GPT models. Chain-of-Thought reasoning did not reduce, and instead increased, overclaiming. AI systems can mimic human self-enhancement and self-protection, raising implications for the emergence of motivated self-like behavior in non-biological systems, the assumed neutrality of LLMs, and the need for improved mitigation techniques.

item.title: Hybrid Human-AI Creativity: Navigating the Affordance Landscape of Creative Exploration
item.description:
Creativity Research Journal
The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems capable of producing text, images, music, and design artifacts has intensified debates about the nature of creativity and the locus of creative agency. Current discussions often frame these technologies either as replacing human creativity or as merely augmenting human creative processes. Such perspectives remain theoretically limited because they conceptualize creativity primarily as an individual cognitive ability rather than a distributed process embedded within sociocultural and material environments. Drawing on ecological approaches to cognition and contemporary creativity research, this paper proposes a conceptual framework that reconceptualizes human-AI creativity as navigation within an expanded affordance landscape. Integrating classical creativity process models with sociocultural and distributed perspectives, GenAI systems are conceptualized as affordance-modulating artifacts that reshape the topology of creative exploration. The framework explains how generative systems expand ideational possibility through rapid combinatorial generation while also influencing creative trajectories through algorithmic anchoring. Eight theoretical propositions link AI-mediated affordances to stages of the creative process. The paper extends distributed creativity theory to technologically mediated environments and outlines a research agenda for empirically investigating hybrid human-AI creativity systems.

item.title: From generation to judgment: the multidimensional structure of design thinking mindset and differences across learning stages in AIGC-supported fashion film design learning
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) is changing how design alternatives are generated in fashion film design learning, enabling students to obtain large numbers of comparable and iteratively refinable visual outcomes within a short period. However, expanded generative capacity does not, by itself, determine how learners interpret, evaluate, experiment with, and select among uncertain outcomes. In this human–AI collaborative creative environment, empirical evidence remains limited on whether learners’ design-related psychological tendencies form a distinguishable multidimensional structure that is comparable across learning stages. Design Thinking Mindset (DTM) provides a multidimensional psychological framework for addressing this issue. Methods Drawing on Vignoli et al.’s DTM framework, this study examined five dimensions—Uncertainty and Risk, Empathy, Experimentation, Abductive Reasoning, and Creative Confidence—through a cross-sectional survey of 409 first-year and third-year students from three Chinese universities who had experience with AIGC fashion film design projects. Confirmatory factor analysis and measurement invariance testing across year groups were used to examine the five-dimensional structure and its measurement comparability, followed by latent mean comparisons. Results The five DTM dimensions formed a correlated yet distinguishable structure and demonstrated measurement comparability across year groups. Third-year students had significantly higher latent means on all five dimensions, with the largest descriptive standardized difference point estimates observed for Abductive Reasoning and Creative Confidence. Discussion These findings provide empirical support for the applicability of five selected DTM dimensions in AIGC-supported fashion film design learning and reveal distinct patterns of self-reported psychological tendencies across year groups. From an educational perspective, the results suggest that AIGC-supported design education should attend not only to the generation of creative alternatives but also to learners’ psychological orientations toward uncertainty, experimentation, audience understanding, creative reasoning, and confidence in creative work.

item.title: Uneven automation: comparing authorship anxiety and generative AI use among art and design undergraduate students
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Art and design education expects students to develop a sense of authorship over original work, but generative AI (GenAI) complicates how students understand and claim that authorship. This study examined whether these experiences differ across creative fields through a mixed-methods design. The survey included 2,441 GenAI-using students from seven field categories at 33 art and design institutions in China and assessed authorship anxiety, creative agency, perceived usefulness, dependence on GenAI, and frequency of use. The quantitative analysis first examined variation across all seven categories and then compared fine art with the five applied design fields. Interview data from 22 survey participants were also examined thematically. The main findings include that (1) authorship anxiety did not differ significantly across the seven categories or between fine art and pooled design; the latter comparison met the equivalence criterion at ±d = 0.20, but not at tighter bounds; (2) clearer differences emerged in how students used GenAI. Compared with fine-art students, design students considered GenAI more useful and used it more frequently; (3) across the interviews, most students described authorship as retaining control over the creative idea while delegating parts of its execution to GenAI. Specifically, fine-art students often grounded authorship in embodied making and human imperfection, whereas design students placed greater emphasis on judgement, selection, and control. We call this pattern uneven automation: concern about authorship was broadly shared, but students in different fields responded to GenAI in different ways, potentially reflecting the varying labour-market pressures surrounding their disciplines.

item.title: Anxiety as fuel? FoMO-AI and employee creativity through creative process engagement: the moderating roles of growth mindset and critical thinking
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Using the transactional theory of stress and coping (TTSC) as an overarching stressor–response framework, compensatory control theory (CCT) to explain compensatory engagement, and conservation of resources (COR) theory to explain resource-based boundary conditions, this study examines whether fear of missing out on artificial intelligence (FoMO-AI) is associated with self-reported employee creativity through creative process engagement (CPE) and whether growth mindset and critical thinking condition this indirect association. A three-wave, time-lagged survey was conducted with 320 employees recruited through the Credamo platform in China. The hypothesized model, which did not include a direct FoMO-AI-to-creativity path, was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap samples. A separately estimated direct-path sensitivity model and necessary condition analysis (NCA) provided complementary assessments. In the hypothesized model, FoMO-AI was positively associated with CPE (β = 0.461, p < 0.001), CPE was positively associated with creativity (β = 0.520, p < 0.001), and the hypothesized indirect effect was 0.240 ( p < 0.001). The FoMO-AI–CPE association was stronger at higher levels of growth mindset (β = 0.505, p < 0.001), and the CPE–creativity association was stronger at higher levels of critical thinking (β = 0.190, p = 0.002). The results supported a first-stage moderated mediation pattern and conditionally supported a second-stage moderated mediation pattern, which was significant at the mean and high levels of growth mindset but not at the low level. In the separately estimated direct-path sensitivity model, the added FoMO-AI-to-creativity path (β = 0.417, p < 0.001) and the corresponding indirect effect through CPE (β = 0.197, p < 0.001) were significant, whereas the critical-thinking interaction was nonsignificant (β = 0.042, p = 0.321). Estimates from the sensitivity model were not used to evaluate the hypotheses. NCA identified moderate, sample-bound necessity effects for CPE (CR-FDH: d = 0.173, p < 0.001) and critical thinking (CR-FDH: d = 0.109, p = 0.034), whereas the effect for growth mindset was nonsignificant. These necessity results do not imply sufficiency or causality. The single-country, non-probability platform sample, panel attrition, reliance on self-reports, and lack of direct measures of stress appraisal and coping limit causal, population-level, and cross-cultural generalization. The findings should therefore be interpreted as sample-bound associations among the retained Chinese employees. Future research should use organizational, probability-based, and cross-national samples, collect supervisor-rated or behavioral creativity outcomes, and examine appraisal and coping processes directly. This study identifies an indirect association between FoMO-AI and self-reported creativity through CPE and clarifies stage-specific, resource-based boundary conditions. The separately estimated direct-path sensitivity model reveals a residual FoMO-AI–creativity association and indicates that the critical-thinking result is model-dependent, thereby qualifying a uniformly beneficial interpretation of FoMO-AI.

item.title: CogChat: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Conversational AI with Heterogeneous Graph Transformer for Cognitive Grounding in Design Generation
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
LLM-based chat systems have become valuable tools for design practice, enabling rapid ideation and flexible task support. Yet these systems process designer utterances as generic sequences, maintaining context through recency rather than through any model of how the speaker organizes knowledge. In design conversation, this gap compounds as relational context decays between turns, identical words go unresolved across designers, and the conversation loops or restarts rather than deepens. We present CogChat, a real-time chat framework that grounds conversational AI in a personal heterogeneous knowledge graph constructed from each designer’s input. The system extracts typed entities and relations into a heterogeneous graph, then applies a HGT (Heterogeneous Graph Transformer) to select structurally relevant nodes for response generation and to generate both intentional and exploratory probing questions. Technical evaluation shows that HGT-based entity selection outperforms both ungrounded LLM interaction and naïve KG augmentation, which introduces noise that degrades response quality. A within-subjects study with nine professional designers indicates that grounding conversation in a relationally structured, designer-specific semantic context improves context retention, personalized intent interpretation, and conversational depth while reducing cognitive load. These findings suggest that structuring a designer’s expressed concepts and relations as a dynamic knowledge graph can preserve relational context that fades across turns, pointing toward a graph-grounded approach to long-term context management in LLM-based interaction.

item.title: ImageDirector: Expressing Spatial Intent via 3D Direct Manipulation for Generative Image Editing
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Generative image editing through text prompting suffers from two fundamental limitations: text is imprecise for specifying spatial changes, and iterative edits often introduce unwanted visual drift. In contrast, people naturally approach image editing with a compositor’s intuition: manipulating individual objects while expecting the rest of the scene to remain intact. We present ImageDirector, a generative image editing system that supports this intuition by enabling users to manipulate objects in a 2D generated image as if they exist in 3D space. Given a generated image, our system segments a selected object, turns it into a manipulable high-fidelity 3D proxy via image-to-3D lifting, and lets users reposition, rotate, and scale it through direct manipulation. The system then re-composites and harmonizes the result with background regions preserved. In a within-subjects study (N = 12), ImageDirector significantly outperformed a text-only prompting baseline in spatial accuracy and visual consistency across iterative edits; participants also reported substantially greater perceived control and expressiveness over the editing process. Finally, we discuss how this approach extends to broader content creation workflows, opening new possibilities for intuitive, precise, and controllable human-AI co-creation.

item.title: Treellis: Exposing Editable Assembly Structures for Progressive Human-AI Co-Creation of 3D Models
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Generative AI lowers the barriers to 3D modeling but offers limited control over outcomes. We present Treellis, a human-AI co-creation tool for 3D modeling. Given a text prompt, Treellis produces a 3D object along with a user interface that reveals its component-level assembly structure and in-situ editable parameters. This enables users to inspect and iteratively refine problematic regions of the model at multiple levels of granularity using both AI-assisted operations and direct manual edits, while preserving usable substructures unaffected. Across a between-subject controlled study and a multi-session open-ended study, we found that Treellis helped users develop efficient hybrid strategies between AI and manual to create complex 3D designs. Results also show that exposing AI-generated 3D artifacts as editable assembly structures can support localized repair and reduce refinement friction in human-AI 3D co-creation.

item.title: Social.Wiki: A Web Held in Common
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Many of the websites people depend on have owners whose interests are not fully aligned with their users. We address the root of this problem by presenting a reimagining of the web where sites are not owned at all but are instead collaboratively produced like Wikipedia articles. We call the system Social.Wiki because it supports the co-creation of interactive social sites, such as those for microblogging, messaging, dating, gaming, ride sharing, and so on. With off-the-shelf AI tools, people with little or no programming experience can edit these sites to better reflect the needs and preferences of their communities. Social.Wiki builds on ideas from collaborative malleable software systems such as Webstrates, but is designed for public participation rather than use only within small, trusted groups. To this end, Social.Wiki includes governance to mitigate conflict. To accommodate diverse governance preferences, our model of “ plural governance ” lets people independently choose the policies that determine which edits to a site they see. Social.Wiki also implements a granular security model to protect personal data in a malleable environment. Complementing the decentralized design and governance of Social.Wiki sites, both site edits and within-site data are stored on Graffiti, a decentralized infrastructure, decoupling the ownership of underlying servers from the ownership of sites. We evaluate Social.Wiki through case studies that demonstrate the range of sociotechnical structures it supports, as well as through deployments at a hackathon and in the wild.

item.title: "What Are You Really Trying to Do?": Co-Creating Life Goals from Everyday Computer Use
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Recent advances in user modeling make it feasible to conduct open-ended inference over a person’s everyday computer use. Despite longstanding visions of systems that deeply understand our actions and the purposes they serve in our lives, existing systems only capture what a person is doing in the moment, not why they are doing it, limiting these systems to surface-level support. We introduce striving co-creation, a process for inferring broader life goals from unstructured observations of computer use. Grounded in Activity Theory and Emmons’ personal strivings framework, our system progressively constructs a hierarchical representation of a person’s activities. Strivings are, however, difficult to fully resolve from observation alone, as the same action can be driven by many different goals. Our system therefore supports an editing interface that gives people agency over how they are understood by the system, feeding their corrections back into subsequent rounds of striving induction. In a week-long field deployment (N = 14), we find that our co-creation process produces strivings that participants recognize as representative of their long-term goals and gives them greater agency than baseline methods.

item.title: Narrative Keyframing for Generative Creative Writing
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
We introduce narrative keyframing, an interaction technique for AI-assisted creative writing that lets writers specify different types of narrative constraints at selected moments in a story, then use AI to generate intervening prose. Inspired by the use of keyframing in animation, narrative keyframing offers a flexible way to connect story planning with adaptive control over generated text. We explore three types of keyframes: plot keyframes define significant events in a story, character keyframes represent how individual characters change over the narrative, and perspective keyframes capture how individual characters experience different events through first-person narratives. Plot and character keyframes offer a flexible way to adapt the type of high-level conditioning explored in previous AI writing tools to more customizable, iterative, and fine-scale control, while perspective keyframes add a new way to control characterization and focalization by using first-person narratives as an intermediary. Through a user study, we show that narrative keyframing supports a more controllable, transparent, and engaging way to use generative AI in creative writing.

item.title: FabDreamer: Exploring the Image-to-Physical Workflow Through AI-Assisted Layered Fabrication
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Generative AI lets anyone create rich visual content in seconds, yet translating that content into a physically fabricable artifact still demands manual decomposition, occlusion repair, and structural verification that most tools leave entirely to the user. We present FabDreamer, an image-to-physical system that carries an image to fabrication-ready SVGs through three stages with deliberately staged AI initiative: (1) AI leads decomposition into depth-ordered layers, (2) assists on demand during creative editing with real-time 3D preview, and (3) advises on structural integrity before export. We instantiate this workflow for layered laser-cut art and evaluate it through three rounds including a formative analysis, an early prototype user evaluation (N=13), and a cross-domain practitioner study with specialists from 6 fabrication domains (N=6). Our findings show that physical awareness during design opens creative opportunities beyond error prevention, that practitioners appropriate the system’s generic geometric operations for their own domains, and that the fabrication agent covers geometry-readable constraints while domain knowledge remains with the maker.

item.title: VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Great fiction earns its verisimilitude through precise details, from how a longsword is gripped to pierce armor gaps to why a bleeding corpse cannot yet smell of decay, weaving domain expertise into the fabric of invented worlds. Current AI writing tools offer limited support for discovering and integrating unfamiliar domain knowledge into narrative. They require explicit queries that authors cannot formulate, generate finished prose that risks homogenizing voice, or assist only within the boundaries of what authors already know. We argue that AI should reveal latent knowledge gaps to writers while preserving their agency to transform discovered knowledge into authentic prose. Grounded in formative interviews with 9 fiction writers, we present VeriForge, a mixed-initiative writing system that divides cognitive labor so that the system assumes initiative over domain discovery while the author retains full initiative over narrative synthesis. VeriForge realizes this through three complementary mechanisms. Proactive inline highlighting flags potential knowledge gaps as authors draft. Dual-stream querying pairs conversational responses with source-anchored Knowledge Cards for direct fact extraction. A spatial Knowledge Canvas allows authors to organize and connect discovered knowledge across their writing. These mechanisms are powered by a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation pipeline grounded in domain-specific source materials. A within-subjects user study (N=12) provides preliminary evidence that this paradigm helps authors recognize previously overlooked knowledge gaps, supports creative exploration, and is perceived by expert raters to produce passages with stronger domain grounding in a controlled cold-start writing task.

item.title: DocuDebug: A Graph-Supported Interactive Editor for Verifying and Maintaining Internal Logical Consistency
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
While large language models (LLMs) accelerate report generation, maintaining logical consistency during revisions increases the cognitive load, and delegating this task to LLMs often results in unpredictable global overwrites. To address this, we present DocuDebug, an interactive editor that reframes document verification as a software engineering task. The system models a document’s logical structure and citations as an explicit dependency graph. Through a linter-like interface, users receive real-time warnings for logical conflicts and propagate localized edits with guided precision. In a within-subjects study with 12 professional writers, DocuDebug guided precise, necessary corrections, improving precision over threefold and reducing over-editing from over 40% to under 5%. Furthermore, objective logs revealed that users avoided blind acceptance, actively deliberating over each warning for nearly three minutes. This work demonstrates how structured visual diagnostics can shift AI-assisted writing from opaque global generation to systematic, user-controlled co-creation.

item.title: Micro-Edits: Computational Support for Fine-Scale Edits in Film
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
In film editing, every frame matters. While macro, content-level edits shape the high-level narrative of a film, small local edits often control timing and direct visual attention. For example, editors can adjust the precise timing of clips to control the length of a meaningful silence, or cut to shots that highlight a specific character’s reactions to important moments. These small, detailed edits are slow and tedious to make in standard editing tools because users have to map high-level narrative goals to low-level frame-by-frame adjustments. At the same time, these fine-scale adjustments, which we call micro-edits, can be nuanced and expressive, with different choices serving different creative goals. In this work, we start by conducting a formative study with professional editors to understand the structure of micro-edits and how they are used. We then derive a mathematical formalization for this structure to develop tools that leverage AI and optimization to make exploring micro-edits simpler and more efficient for users. Finally, we validate our tools in multiple user studies and a wide range of video examples.

item.title: MAIC-UI: Making Interactive Courseware with Generative UI
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Creating interactive STEM courseware traditionally requires HTML/CSS/JavaScript expertise, leaving barriers for educators. While generative AI can produce HTML codes, existing tools generate static presentations rather than interactive simulations, struggle with long documents, and lack pedagogical accuracy mechanisms. Furthermore, full regeneration for modifications requires 200–600 seconds, disrupting creative flow. We present MAIC-UI, a zero-code authoring system that enables educators to create and rapidly edit interactive courseware from textbooks, PPTs, and PDFs. MAIC-UI employs: (1) structured knowledge analysis with multi-modal understanding to ensure pedagogical rigor; (2) a two-stage generate-verify-optimize pipeline separating content alignment from visual refinement; and (3) Click-to-Locate editing with Unified Diff-based incremental generation achieving sub-10-second iteration cycles. A controlled lab study with 40 participants shows MAIC-UI reduces editing iterations (4.9 vs. 7.0) and significantly improves learnability and controllability compared to direct Text-to-HTML generation. A three-month classroom deployment with 53 high school students demonstrates that MAIC-UI fosters learning agency and reduces outcome disparities—the pilot class achieved 9.21-point gains in STEM subjects compared to -2.32 points in control classes. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-MAIC/MAIC-UI.

item.title: Map2Video: Guiding Real-World-Grounded AI Video Generation
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
AI video generation lowers barriers to video creation, but existing tools provide limited support for grounding content in real-world locations, restricting their use in applications such as film previsualization and scenario generation. In practice, users rely on verbose textual descriptions or reference images using on-site photos or street view imagery (SVI), which are cumbersome and unreliable across shots. Our formative study with five filmmakers revealed challenges in shot composition, character motion, and camera control when using SVI with an image-to-video tool. We present Map2Video, a system for guiding SVI-grounded AI video generation through map-based character trajectory annotation and direct manipulation of cameras and character masks defined in geodetic coordinates and projected onto panoramic screen coordinates. In an evaluation with twelve filmmakers, Map2Video provided stronger controllability for both scene replication and open-ended creative exploration, reduced cognitive effort, and improved spatial consistency across multiple shots compared to an image-to-video baseline.

item.title: MultiVerse: A Creator-Centered Approach to Steering Context-Adaptive Lyrics
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Generative AI may enable new forms of context-aware creative expression by dynamically tailoring media content to its consumption context. For instance, AI systems could adapt song lyrics to the listener and their current activity. However, existing media adaptation systems primarily optimize for audience experience, often neglecting artists’ intent, style, and preference. We address this challenge by introducing a novel creator-centered approach to adaptive media authoring and present MultiVerse, a system that instantiates this approach for steering adaptive lyrics. Our approach allows creators to explicitly author controls based on their intent, lyric structure, and audience context, and uses rule-based validations to ensure controls are followed. We conducted a study with 10 songwriters, comparing MultiVerse with a prompting-based workflow for composing adaptive lyrics. The comparison revealed that creators preferred to author how lyrics adapt by explicitly specifying relevant context and adaptation constraints, while recognizing trade-offs in flexibility and iteration speed. Interviews further revealed that creators viewed adaptive media as enabling new forms of audience connection, introducing a distinct creative process, favoring new compositional strategies, and reshaping notions of authorship.

item.title: PartInteractor: Intent-Driven Part-Aware 3D Authoring for Continuous Co-Creation in XR
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
As Extended Reality (XR) evolves into an immersive computing medium, interactive 3D authoring becomes essential for creative and functional workflows. However, existing generative XR systems produce monolithic outputs lacking explicit semantic structure, limiting post-generation control. We introduce PartInteractor, a representation-to-interaction framework that investigates how semantic part hierarchies can be incorporated into generative XR authoring, and exposed as first-class, directly manipulable units, turning one-shot prompt-to-object generation into continuous component-level co-creation. PartInteractor supports speech, sketch, and image inputs, integrating an LLM interpreter with a retrieval-generation strategy to scaffold user intent prior to 3D generation. Instead of producing monolithic objects, our system generates semantically decomposed 3D assets with explicit part hierarchies, enabling rich component-level interaction over object structure and composition. Our evaluations suggest that part-aware representation increases post-generation control and reduces reliance on whole-object regeneration, while intent scaffolding mitigates ambiguity and improves intent-result alignment, together supporting more expressive and controllable human-AI co-creation workflows. These results highlight part-aware representation and intent scaffolding as promising design considerations for future generative XR authoring systems.

item.title: Supporting creative agency: metacognitive control and trust in generative AI art education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
This paper employs a quantitative multimethod design to extend the UTAUT framework for generative AI (GenAI) adoption among art students. Study 1 tested the integrated model via structural equation modeling using cross-sectional survey data from 450 Chinese art students and developed a trust construct grounded in instrumental technology trust, supplemented by art-value-aligned items. Trust in GenAI showed the strongest direct association with behavioral intention ( β = 0.425). Social influence was the dominant correlate of trust ( β = 0.262), with 42.1% of its total effect mediated indirectly through trust. Metacognitive control showed a positive direct association with behavioral intention ( β = 0.146), alongside an indirect association through trust. The structural model based on survey data explained 59.7% of the variance in behavioral intention. Study 2 used a between-subjects experiment with 80 art students to test whether situational metacognitive prompting causally affected creative output. Participants receiving metacognitive prompts (Group A) obtained higher expert ratings than the control group (Group B) on semantic content ( d = 0.67), visual style ( d = 1.30), and spatial composition ( d = 0.63); within-group feature-distance analyses also indicated greater output diversity in Group A across all three dimensions. These findings suggest that trust and metacognitive control are key pathways in GenAI adoption for artistic creation, and that low-cost situational metacognitive prompting may enhance both the quality and diversity of AI-assisted artworks.

item.title: Learning engagement and creative self-beliefs in generative AI-supported design education: self-reported prompt literacy and dimensions of AI dependence
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative AI (GenAI) is changing how design students learn, yet little is known about how students’ perceived capability to work with GenAI relates to their learning engagement and motivational self-beliefs, or under which forms of AI dependence this link is weaker. Drawing on social cognitive theory, this cross-sectional study examined self-reported prompt literacy, learning engagement, and two components of the creative self: creative self-efficacy (CSE), a motivational belief in one’s creative capability, and creative personal identity (CPI), the importance of creativity to one’s self-concept. Survey data came from 829 undergraduate art and design students in 40 intact classes at two institutions in mainland China; latent-variable and moderation models accounted for the clustering of students within classes. Self-reported prompt literacy was positively associated with engagement ( β = 0.54), and engagement was positively associated with both CSE ( β = 0.62) and CPI ( β = 0.47). Engagement was more strongly associated with CSE than with CPI (difference = 0.14, 95% CI [0.04, 0.24]) and remained uniquely associated with CPI after CSE was taken into account. When four dimensions of AI dependence were modeled simultaneously, the prompt literacy–engagement association was weaker among students reporting higher cognitive dependence; evidence for loss of control was weaker, and functional and emotional dependence showed no clear unique moderation. All interaction effects were small. The dimensional analysis identified cognitive dependence as the clearest moderator. These cross-sectional, self-reported findings suggest possible boundary conditions for the capability–engagement association and require longitudinal and behavioral testing.

item.title: Owning what one did not make: psychological ownership, agency, and the authorship legitimation deficit in human–AI co-creation
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Authorship can align three relations to a work: experiencing it as one’s own, feeling like the agent behind it, and standing answerable for it. Effortful engagement can support this alignment, an arrangement this article calls the labor nexus of authorship, but direction, selection, editing, and authority over release also matter. Generative artificial intelligence can separate initial-production effort from the resulting product without uniformly weakening ownership, agency, or responsibility. This conceptual analysis specifies an authorship legitimation deficit as a mismatch between a particular authorship designation and the experiential or contribution-based grounds expected to support it under prior domain criteria. Separate ownership, agency, and community-warrant profiles distinguish an unsupported sole-creator claim from a supported editorial role, even when the person’s contribution and experience are unchanged. Historical precedents locate the problem within delegated and distributed making. The main contribution is a role-relative conceptual classification. Conditional relational hypotheses concern refusal or qualification of authorship (P4) and later recognition of alternative contributions (P6); agency and observer credit-blame hypotheses (P5a/P5b) concern constituent concepts rather than effects of the deficit. Market dependence suppresses observable disavowal when qualification threatens income; perceived system agency conditions felt answerability while assigned release duties remain fixed. Contribution records may assist later recognition but do not guarantee it. The framework identifies when a role exceeds its grounds while preserving supported AI-assisted authorship and accountability for release.

item.title: Will AI Solve It All? A Transnational Qualitative Investigation of AI’s Role in Human Needs Fulfillment
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Artificial intelligence is increasingly promoted as a transformative solution for addressing fundamental human needs and improving quality of life. However, limited empirical research examines what people expect from AI in relation to their needs and how current AI technologies are perceived to meet them. This study presents a transnational qualitative investigation of AI’s role in human needs fulfillment across six countries. Guided by Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, findings show that recurring concerns about inaccuracy, hallucination, and trust point to informational integrity as an emerging need in AI-mediated contexts. Participants also viewed AI as a supportive tool rather than a replacement for human agency and creativity. Cross-national patterns showed a shared desire for personalized, adaptive AI, while the domains participants emphasized varied by country, reflecting local priorities. This work underscores the need to ground AI evaluation in lived experience and expand theoretical perspectives to account for evolving dimensions of human needs.

item.title: Who is more likely to use generative AI? Differences among students with and without disabilities across U.S. colleges and universities
item.description:
Computers in Human Behavior Reports
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly become an everyday technology, but little is known about how its use is distributed across populations or the implications for digital equity. College students with disabilities encounter distinct challenges as they manage their academic, health, social, and creative needs. The flexible, on-demand nature of GenAI might help them in ways that are different from how it supports the general student population. Using a large multi-institution sample of U.S. college students ( N = 104,729), we examined GenAI use across five domains (health-related issues, academic-related matters, non-academic work, personal communications, and creative work for fun) between students with and without disabilities. Results from multivariable logistic regression showed that students with disabilities were significantly more likely than students without disabilities to use GenAI across all five domains, with the largest disparities observed for creative work for fun (aOR = 1.53; 95% CI: 1.42–1.65; p < 0.001), health-related issues (aOR = 1.47; 95% CI: 1.31–1.65; p < 0.001), and personal communications (aOR = 1.44; 95% CI: 1.30–1.58; p < 0.001), adjusting for demographics. In exploratory analyses, we observed variation in GenAI use across disability types, with students with ADHD, psychological disorders, neurological disorders, and learning disorders having the highest prevalence, and students with mobility impairments reporting the lowest. The findings suggest a need to support the safe, effective use of GenAI among students who have already adopted it and to promote accessibility of GenAI technologies for students with different disabilities.

item.title: AI in music performance: the human-AI performance loop
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Music is a distinctly human artform, one that has been written, taught, shared, and reinterpreted for thousands of years. The rise of powerful artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping musical creation in ways subtle and profound. Here I propose the human-AI performance loop as a framework for understanding these developments through three principal roles: the AI listener derives musical information from sound and movement; the AI coach guides practice using performance evidence and musicians’ learning goals; and the AI partner performs with the musician in a collaborative dynamic process. With the human musician at the centre of the framework, human → AI → human exchanges become coupled through shared information and musicians’ actions. Evaluating these roles will require multilayered evidence to support their adoption: accurate and musically relevant analysis, demonstrated improvements in musician performance and knowledge through coaching, and effective and supportive coordination between musicians and AI partners. Audience beliefs about AI will also shape reception of the creative output, making musical purpose and honest representation important considerations in an AI music performance system. The human-AI performance loop provides a basis for investigating how these roles can extend support between lessons and rehearsals, broaden opportunities for ensemble performance, and contribute to musicians’ learning and enjoyment of the musical experience.

item.title: Explaining designers’ adoption of AIGC image generation tools: A configurational analysis integrating PLS-SEM and fsQCA
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence is reshaping how concept generation, visual exploration, and solution iteration are organized in design tasks, yet designers’ behavioral intention toward AIGC image-generation tools is difficult to explain through efficiency or ease of use alone. This study places UTAUT2 and the task–technology fit model within a unified analytical framework and incorporates personal innovativeness and design ethics to examine the associations among design task characteristics, AIGC technology characteristics, adoption evaluations, designers’ characteristics, and behavioral intention. Based on questionnaire data from 338 respondents with self-reported prior use of AIGC image-generation tools, this study employs PLS-SEM to examine average associations among variables and combines it with fsQCA to identify configurations associated with high behavioral intention and non-high behavioral intention. The PLS-SEM results show that task–technology fit is significantly and positively associated with behavioral intention, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and price value, while performance expectancy, effort expectancy, hedonic motivation, price value, and habit are also significantly and positively associated with behavioral intention. The direct paths from social influence, facilitating conditions, personal innovativeness, and design ethics do not reach statistical significance; in this study, design ethics mainly concerns awareness of copyright, intellectual property, creative attribution, and transparent use. The baseline fsQCA identifies three configurations associated with high behavioral intention. A2 and A3 combine hedonic motivation with task–technology fit, facilitating conditions, habit, and other conditions and remain under the more stringent case-frequency threshold. A1 contains six cases, has relatively low raw coverage, and disappears when the case-frequency threshold is increased, supporting an exploratory interpretation of this threshold-sensitive configuration. Configurations associated with non-high behavioral intention are not simple reversals of those associated with high behavioral intention. The findings suggest that designers’ evaluations of AIGC are grounded in the fit between technological capabilities and design tasks, while hedonic motivation, task–technology fit, facilitating conditions, price value, and habit occupy different positions across configurations. These findings may provide reference points for AIGC tool development, design organization management, and designer capability development.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence in Embodied Learning: A Systematic Literature Review
item.description:
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
ABSTRACT Background Embodied learning (EL) is an educational approach that posits that cognition develops as learners interact with their environment through physical activity or sensory experiences. Artificial intelligence in education (AIED) supports teaching and learning for both teachers and students, for example through personalised intelligent tutoring systems. However, prior research on EL has focused primarily on students' cognitive and emotional abilities and the integration of body and task, rather than on technological elements, and research on technology‐based embodied learning (TBEL) has centred on immersive technologies such as VR and AR. Objectives This study aims to explore the relationship between AI technology and EL by analysing (1) the types of AI utilised in EL‐related research (algorithm or model, data modality, AI role), (2) learners' outcomes obtained from AI‐based EL, and (3) the limitations and solutions when applying AI to EL. Method This study is a systematic literature review based on the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and no meta‐analysis was conducted. This study only referenced papers published since 2016 that included both AI technology and EL, were written in English, and dealt with learning processes mediated by physical activity. A study was treated as within scope only where the physical activity was tied to the concept to be learned. Papers were excluded if they did not specify the AI algorithm or model, were not peer‐reviewed, were secondary studies, were not in the field of education, were unavailable in full text, emphasised only simple skill acquisition in physical education or music, or emphasised only simple speaking activities in foreign language learning. Searches were conducted on 16 September 2025 in ACM, ERIC, and Web of Science. Given the diverse types of included studies, risk of bias was assessed using the MMAT2018 tool. Due to the varied nature of the data, a multi‐faceted data synthesis was performed. Co‐occurrences between data modality and AI role, and between AI role and learner outcomes, were visualised using heatmaps. The flow between the three variables was represented using a Sankey diagram. Finally, all frequencies were recalculated after excluding papers appraised as Low or not appraised, to test which patterns depended on weaker evidence. Results A total of 23 papers were reviewed. As multiple data points could be extracted per item, the relative proportion was calculated against the number of coding instances per item. The most frequently used AI algorithm/model in the EL context was deep learning, and the data modality was image data. Where multiple data types were used, it was tagged as multimodal, accounting for 34.8%. Analysis and evaluation roles were most frequently extracted, and cognitive outcomes were reported most often. Key limitations identified included restricted participant numbers due to research design and studies conducted in controlled environments. Among papers appraised as High, the most frequent pathways ran from multimodal data to recognition and detection and from sensor data to analysis and evaluation, and cognitive outcomes were the most frequently reported. When papers appraised as Low or not appraised were set aside, the concentration of AI in analytical roles persisted, whereas the evidence for AI as an interactive or generative participant weakened. Discussion This review describes reported patterns rather than pooled effect estimates, as no meta‐analysis was conducted. Exclusion of grey literature may introduce publication bias. Furthermore, the potential risk of selection bias exists as literature was collected based on inclusion/exclusion criteria. This study is significant in that it identified how AI is utilised within the EL context and the learner outcomes reported alongside it, particularly as the scope of AIED broadens.

item.title: Psychological mechanisms of perceived technological dependence on generative artificial intelligence tools: perceived knowledge, trust, anxiety, and self-efficacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative AI tools are increasingly used in design education, yet the relationship between students’ perceptions of these tools and their reported reliance on them remains unclear. This study analyzed cross-sectional survey responses from 526 undergraduate students in design-related disciplines using partial least squares structural equation modeling. In the specified model, perceived reliability, perceived usefulness, and perceived intelligence were positively associated with perceived AIGC knowledge, whereas perceived ease of use was not significantly associated with it. Perceived AIGC knowledge was positively associated with trust, self-efficacy, and usage intention and negatively associated with AIGC-related anxiety. Trust, AIGC-related anxiety, and self-efficacy each showed a significant indirect effect in the modeled relationship between perceived AIGC knowledge and usage intention. Usage intention was strongly associated with perceived technological dependence. These findings are consistent with the proposed framework, but the cross-sectional data do not establish the temporal sequence of the constructs or show that reported dependence reflects harmful overuse. The study extends technology acceptance research by examining perceived reliance in AIGC-supported creative work.

item.title: "Catching lightning in a bottle": How Blind or Low Vision Creators Navigate Ideation Across Creative Domains
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Ideation, i.e., generating, capturing, organizing, and evaluating ideas, is foundational to creative practices; yet little is known about how blind and low vision (BLV) creators engage in ideation. We conducted interviews with 20 BLV creators working in different domains including poetry, music production, tactile graphics, digital drawing, and mixed-media arts. Our findings reveal how participants established accessible creative workflows under social and institutional constraints, drew inspiration from diverse physical and digital sources, captured and organized ideas across text, audio, visual, and physical modalities, and evaluated their work through human and AI feedback. We discuss how ableist norms and accessibility breakdowns cascade across ideation pathways, progressively narrowing BLV individuals’ creative possibilities. Finally, we offer design considerations for building accessible ideation support tools that amplify BLV creators’ distinctive practices.

item.title: Synthesizing and Evaluating a Visual Feedback Framework for Accessible Content Creation
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Many blind and low-vision (BLV) individuals are interested in visual content creation, yet creative tools provide limited feedback for visual outputs during authoring. We synthesized and evaluated a visual feedback framework for creative tasks—we first conducted a purpose-specific literature review of 54 accessibility papers on BLV creators’ feedback needs and then refined the resulting framework through expert review interviews with nine BLV creators. We identify key feedback components for creative work, including object and people information, spatial layout, intent-based checking and suggestions, version differences, and visual aesthetics. We also outline delivery guidelines emphasizing hierarchical control, multimodal interaction, real-time verification, non-visual language, and transparency about AI accuracy. Our findings show that creative authoring requires more detailed and intent-driven feedback than passive consumption, particularly to support iterative decision-making and diverse creative goals. Rather than a prescriptive checklist, this framework offers a practical foundation for researchers and practitioners when designing and evaluating accessible creative tools.

item.title: Gendered affective representations in AI-assisted music videos: a qualitative multimethod study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly visible in music-video production, influencing both production practices and the ways in which emotion, bodies, and gender are portrayed visually. This study examines gendered emotional representation in AI-assisted music videos. Methods A qualitative multimethod design combined interpretive visual analysis of four purposively selected AI-assisted music videos with asynchronous written expert interviews involving six creative-industry professionals and four psychology experts ( N = 10). The videos were analysed through an interpretive coding framework covering emotion, gender, body and face, power relations, AI aesthetics, and traces of bias. Results Across the cases, emotion was conveyed not only through facial expression but also through atmosphere, colour, movement, editing, and spatial transitions. The selected works sometimes reproduced familiar conventions, including heteronormative intimacy, militarised masculinity, and idealised female bodies, but also unsettled them through female anger and solidarity and mutable synthetic bodies. Ambiguity in a body’s appearance did not necessarily unsettle its gendered narrative role. Industry accounts described how prompting, selection, revision, and post-production shape representations, while general psychology-expert perspectives informed their interpretation. Discussion The findings position AI-assisted music videos as co-produced sites of synthetic visual culture in which established gendered conventions may be repeated, negotiated, or challenged. Neither expert group provided direct evidence about the production or reception of the selected videos. The findings underline the practical importance of representational review, consent, diversity, and transparent disclosure in AI-assisted cultural production.

item.title: Parasocial and interpersonal interaction: distinct associations with customer value co-creation in virtual brand communities
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Virtual brand communities expose members to communication from the brand side and interaction with other members, but these sources may not relate to participation through the same psychological processes. Drawing on the stimulus organism response framework, social identity theory, and social cognitive theory, this study tested whether community identification and self-efficacy statistically accounted for indirect associations between parasocial interaction, interpersonal interaction, and customer value co-creation behavior. The hypotheses were examined in an unpublished cross-sectional survey of 240 adult users of virtual brand communities in China. An audit of the questionnaire and data codebook corrected a prior item-block parsing error and established the intended 30-item measurement structure. Internal consistency was acceptable for the five composites (Cronbach's alpha = 0.730–0.837; McDonald's omega = 0.744–0.838). A five-factor confirmatory model fit better than models combining the interaction constructs, combining the mediators, or placing all items on one factor, although its absolute fit and discriminant validity were only partly satisfactory (CFI = 0.870, TLI = 0.857, RMSEA = 0.064, SRMR = 0.056). Regression estimates used HC3 robust standard errors, and indirect associations used 5,000 percentile-bootstrap samples. Parasocial interaction uniquely predicted community identification and self-efficacy, and both variables were associated with customer value co-creation. The indirect associations of parasocial interaction through community identification ( B = 0.163, 95% CI [0.038, 0.303]) and self-efficacy ( B = 0.167, 95% CI [0.053, 0.281]) were statistically detectable. Interpersonal interaction retained a direct association with customer value co-creation but did not uniquely predict either proposed mediator when both interaction variables were included; its two specific indirect associations were not statistically detectable. Results were similar after excluding uniform responders and after adding demographic and community-use controls. The findings distinguish relational and capability-related correlates of parasocial interaction while showing that interpersonal interaction may share substantial variance with brand-side relational experience. Because the data are cross-sectional, same-source, and affected by incomplete discriminant validity, the indirect effects are interpreted as covariance patterns consistent with the proposed pathways rather than evidence of causal psychological mechanisms.

item.title: Prompt specificity and iterative behaviour in text-to-music co-creation: a secondary analysis of interaction logs and a framework for perceived creative control
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence can lower barriers to musical creation while also shifting consequential decisions away from the user. Methods This study examines that tension through a secondary analysis of the published PAGURI interaction-log prompt corpus and develops a tentative framework for perceived creative control. The analysable corpus contained 304 text-to-music prompts from 24 participants. Musical specificity was operationalised as explicit instrument and technical-parameter markers; iterative continuity was measured with Jaccard similarity between consecutive prompts and checked against TF-IDF cosine similarity. To avoid pseudoreplication, group comparisons were conducted on participant-level summaries rather than treating 304 prompts as independent cases. Results Role-derived experience groups differed substantially in mean prompt specificity, H(2) = 10.25, p = 0.006, ε 2 = 0.39, and specificity density, H(2) = 11.52, p = 0.003, ε 2 = 0.45, but not in refinement rate, H(2) = 0.24, p = 0.888. At a descriptive Jaccard threshold of 0.20, 46.8% of consecutive pairs were refinements and 53.2% were restarts; because this classification was threshold-sensitive, continuous similarity remained the primary continuity measure. Prompt specificity did not increase systematically across the session: the mean within-person Spearman correlation was ρ = −0.06, and the distribution of participant-level correlations did not differ significantly from zero, W = 89.0, p = 0.374. Discussion These findings distinguish the explicit technical-musical information users encode in prompts from the sequential continuity of their prompting behaviour. The paper integrates task structure, system autonomy, model coverage, prior experience, self-efficacy, and psychological ownership into a testable framework for future music-education research. Given the small participant-level sample and role-derived grouping, the empirical findings are exploratory and require confirmation in larger, controlled studies.

item.title: How AI disclosure influences consumers' purchase intention toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion: the roles of perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background With the growing application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in fashion design and cultural and creative industries, AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion has created new opportunities for the contemporary transformation of traditional culture. However, whether consumers are willing to accept such products and how AI disclosure influences their evaluations and purchase intentions remain unclear. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model, this study examines the mechanisms through which AI disclosure, design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion influence consumers' purchase intentions toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion. Methods A questionnaire survey combined with a scenario-based experiment was employed. Six AI-generated fashion illustrations derived from Tujia costume elements were developed and selected as stimulus materials. Participants were randomly assigned to either an AI disclosure group or a non-disclosure group. Data were collected through Tencent Questionnaire, yielding 410 valid responses. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Importance–Performance Map Analysis (IPMA) were employed to examine the structural relationships, mediating effects, moderating effects, and practical priorities for improvement. Results Design aesthetics and cultural identity influenced purchase intention through perceived usefulness and perceived authenticity, with perceived usefulness emerging as the strongest predictor of purchase intention. AI disclosure significantly reduced design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, and perceived authenticity. Algorithm aversion did not significantly moderate the relationship between perceived usefulness and purchase intention but significantly strengthened the positive effect of perceived authenticity on purchase intention. Conclusions This study reveals the multiple psychological pathways through which AI disclosure shapes consumers' evaluations of AI-generated ethnic cultural fashion. The findings further indicate that algorithm aversion alters the extent to which consumers rely on authenticity judgments when forming purchase intentions. This study extends the application of the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model to the context of AI-generated cultural products and provides practical implications for balancing AI transparency, cultural authenticity, and the practical value of products.

item.title: Generative AI as a team moderator in CSCL : Facilitating students' multidimensional engagement through adaptive scaffolding for socially shared regulation of learning
item.description:
British Journal of Educational Technology
Abstract Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is essential for successful collaboration, yet effectively scaffolding it remains challenging because regulatory needs are dynamic and context‐dependent. While generative AI (GenAI) offers potential for adaptive support, current applications in collaborative learning largely position it as a content‐oriented tutor for knowledge explanation or idea generation, leaving its role as a process‐oriented team moderator for scaffolding SSRL processes underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 16‐week quasi‐experiment with 64 undergraduates in China, comparing adaptive SSRL scaffolding delivered by a GenAI agent in the adaptive‐SSRL condition with static scaffolding via structured digital worksheets in the static‐SSRL condition. Survey data and group discussion transcripts were analysed using statistical methods and epistemic network analysis. Results indicated several differences in students' multidimensional engagement between the two conditions: (1) Behaviourally, the adaptive‐SSRL group showed significantly higher participation equality, although participation intensity did not differ significantly between groups. (2) Cognitively, the adaptive‐SSRL group demonstrated deeper cognitive engagement, reflected in more advanced cognitive presence phases and more integrative, solution‐oriented discourse patterns. (3) Emotionally, the adaptive‐SSRL group reported significantly higher overall emotional engagement, particularly feeling more relaxed during collaboration and more connected with peers. These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by showing that GenAI can function as an SSRL‐informed team moderator rather than a content‐oriented tutor. They also offer design implications for GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding and human–AI role division in CSCL. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is critical for successful collaboration and is closely associated with the quality of student engagement. While static scaffolds (eg, worksheets) provide a basic regulatory structure, they fail to adapt to the dynamic and emergent needs of collaborating teams. Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for personalised content support, yet its potential as a process‐oriented team moderator remains underexplored. What this paper adds This study introduced SSRLAgent, a GenAI agent grounded in SSRL theory and established principles of collective metacognitive support, to provide adaptive and interactive regulatory scaffolding. In a 16‐week quasi‐experiment, we compared GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding (SSRLAgent) with static scaffolding (structured digital worksheets) in CSCL. Adaptive‐SSRL scaffolding was associated with higher‐quality engagement: greater participation equality, deeper cognitive engagement and higher overall emotional engagement. Implications for practice and/or policy The study underscores the necessity of shifting SSRL scaffolding from static, ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ support to adaptive GenAI interventions to improve collaborative engagement. The findings provide design guidance for developing SSRL agents that are embedded in the shared interaction space and responsive to groups' moment‐to‐moment regulatory needs. The study suggests a productive human–AI division of labour: GenAI agents can support process coordination and regulatory prompting, while teachers and peers remain essential for relationally complex forms of support that collaborative learning requires.

item.title: The mediating role of artificial intelligence perception and creative idea generation in the impact of sustainable leadership on digital transformation and circular economy awareness
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Today, sustainable leadership is a strategic leadership approach that addresses environmental, social, and economic priorities from a holistic perspective while at the same time driving digital transformation processes. The research aims to explain how sustainable leaders mobilize organizational resources, technological infrastructure, and human creativity within the framework of Dynamic Capabilities Theory. Methods The research was conducted on 456 white-collar employees working in small and medium-sized enterprises operating in Giresun, Kars, and Kırşehir provinces. The data collected by the convenience sampling method were analyzed using the PLS-SEM method with the SmartPLS 4.1.1 program. Results The analysis results show that sustainable leadership has significant and positive effects on perceptions of artificial intelligence, the generation of creative ideas, digital transformation, and awareness of the circular economy. It was found that the perception of artificial intelligence (AI) has a significant effect on both digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. It was also determined that creative idea generation has significant effects on digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. The results of the mediation analyses revealed a partial mediating role for all variables. Discussion The findings reveal that sustainable leadership is not limited to the environmental and social responsibility dimension and is a strategic element that directs digital transformation processes, shapes perceptions towards artificial intelligence, and encourages organizational creativity.
